clinicalPearls: Scapular dyskinesis is an alteration in the normal position and movement of the scapula, most often observed as prominence of the medial or inferomedial border during arm elevation and lowering.
It is usually a response to or a contributor to other shoulder pathology rather than a discrete disease, so search for an underlying cause.
The scapula must protract, upwardly rotate and posteriorly tilt to maintain a stable base for the glenohumeral joint and to preserve the subacromial space during elevation.
Common contributors include periscapular muscle weakness or fatigue (notably serratus anterior and lower trapezius), pain inhibition, posterior capsular tightness and altered thoracic posture.
A neurological cause such as long thoracic nerve palsy (serratus anterior) or spinal accessory nerve palsy (trapezius) must be excluded when winging is prominent.
The scapular assistance and scapular retraction tests help demonstrate that correcting scapular mechanics relieves symptoms and predicts response to rehabilitation.
The SICK scapula (scapular malposition, inferomedial border prominence, coracoid pain and dyskinesis) describes an overuse pattern in overhead athletes.

Management is overwhelmingly rehabilitative, restoring scapular control and flexibility and addressing the primary shoulder disorder, with surgery reserved for specific structural or neurological causes.
reference.pathophysiology: Normal shoulder function depends on coordinated scapulothoracic motion that positions the glenoid optimally beneath the humeral head throughout elevation, maintaining the length-tension relationship of the rotator cuff and preserving subacromial clearance. Scapular dyskinesis arises when this coordination is disrupted by muscular, capsular, postural or neurological factors. Weakness or fatigue of the serratus anterior and lower trapezius, imbalance with an overactive upper trapezius, pain-related inhibition, a tight posteroinferior capsule and pectoralis minor, or denervation of the periscapular muscles all alter scapular upward rotation, posterior tilt and external rotation. The malpositioned scapula reduces the subacromial space, alters glenohumeral contact and increases loads on the rotator cuff and static stabilisers, predisposing to or perpetuating impingement, instability and labral pathology. Thus dyskinesis is frequently both a consequence and a driver of other shoulder conditions.
additionalDifferentials: Long thoracic nerve palsy causing serratus anterior winging
Spinal accessory nerve palsy causing trapezius winging
additionalInvestigations: Structured clinical observation of scapular motion from behind during repeated elevation
Scapular assistance and scapular retraction corrective manoeuvres
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies if neurological winging is suspected
Assessment of posterior capsular and pectoralis minor tightness
MRI or ultrasound of the shoulder to identify associated cuff, labral or instability pathology
Cervical spine and neurological assessment when a proximal cause is suspected
redFlags: Prominent static winging suggesting a long thoracic or spinal accessory nerve palsy
Progressive, symmetrical periscapular wasting suggesting an underlying myopathy or dystrophy
A palpable mass beneath the scapula such as an osteochondroma or elastofibroma
Associated neurological deficit or neck pain suggesting cervical or brachial plexus pathology
reference.prognosis: When it accompanies another shoulder disorder, correcting scapular control through targeted rehabilitation improves symptoms and complements treatment of the primary problem, with a generally good outcome. Prognosis depends on the underlying cause, being more guarded when there is an established nerve palsy or a progressive neuromuscular disorder.
pitfalls: Treating scapular dyskinesis as a standalone diagnosis without identifying the underlying shoulder or neurological cause.
Missing a long thoracic or spinal accessory nerve palsy presenting as winging.
Overlooking an underlying muscular dystrophy in bilateral or progressive cases.
Focusing rehabilitation on the glenohumeral joint alone while neglecting periscapular and postural control.
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma
management: Direct treatment at the underlying cause, since dyskinesis is usually secondary to another shoulder disorder rather than a discrete disease
Prescribe scapular-focused rehabilitation strengthening the serratus anterior and lower trapezius and retraining scapular motor control
Stretch a tight posterior capsule and pectoralis minor and correct thoracic posture and kinetic-chain deficits
Treat associated glenohumeral pathology such as rotator cuff, labral, or instability lesions
Identify neurological winging from long thoracic or spinal accessory nerve palsy and manage accordingly, referring for nerve or tendon-transfer surgery when recovery fails
Use scapular assistance and retraction manoeuvres to guide rehabilitation and predict response
